title: A-D-M
hook: adam, adamah (earth), adom (red): the human is earthy

segments.voice: Yesterday, three words for soul: nefesh, ruach, neshamah, and a breath that made a figure alive. Your line was soul is breath. Did one slow breath change an answer? Today, the figure itself, and what it was made of. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-four.

A spade goes into a garden bed in spring and turns over a clump of earth: dark, damp, smelling of rain, a worm sliding out of sight. In Hebrew, that clump is adamah. Now look at the person holding the spade. In Hebrew, that's adam. Same three letters, alef, dalet, mem, with one small sound added for the ground. The gardener and the garden share a root. The Torah doesn't hide this. It builds its first human out of the very word for soil, and then keeps playing with the sound. Today's root is the one that says what we're made of.
screen: `A CLUMP OF EARTH: ADAMAH.` → `THE ONE HOLDING IT: ADAM.` → `THE SAME THREE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: A-D-M. Alef, dalet, mem. Turn it four ways. First, adamah, the ground. In Genesis chapter two, God forms the human, in the King James, "of the dust of the ground." Ground there is adamah. Second, the human: ha-adam. The story names its creature after its material, and some readers bring the pun into English as earthling. The name is a reminder written into the body, and the next chapter says it out loud: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Third, adom, red. Further on in Genesis, Esau comes in from the field, faint with hunger, and begs his brother for the red stew on the fire. Then the text adds: "therefore was his name called Edom." Red, Edom: the Torah makes that pun itself. Some readers go one step further and hear red in adam too, the reddish color of clay. Fourth, what the rabbis did with one clay. The Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin, asks why the human was created as a single person. One answer it gives: for the sake of peace, so that no one could say to another, my ancestor was greater than yours. Everyone traces back to one figure, and that figure traces back to a handful of ground. Nobody's dust is finer than anyone else's. Not the king's, not yours, not anyone's.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch the ground you came from. If there's soil nearby, a garden, a park, a plant pot on the sill, put your fingers into it. If not, a stone, a wooden table, the floor under your feet will do. Settle, and breathe. Feel the texture. Cool or warm, dry or damp, gritty or smooth. Say the two words to yourself, one after the other: adamah, adam. Ground, human. Let the sound of them sit together for a moment. If you pray, you can give thanks for being made of the earth. The bell holds the time.
A-D-M. Alef, dalet, mem: adamah, the ground; adam, the human made from it; and adom, red, the color of the clay and Edom's stew. Today's word.

Your line: human from earth. Today, when someone gets under your skin, remember the Mishnah's point: you're made of the same ground, and neither of your ancestors outranks the other. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Jews read the creation of adam from the adamah in Genesis, and the Mishnah in tractate Sanhedrin teaches from it that humans share one ancestry, so that no one may claim a greater lineage than another.
